analysis.one_liner: Takes congressional redistricting away from state legislators and gives it to appointed commissions.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 5, 1989 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, state legislatures draw the boundaries of congressional districts after each census, which lets the majority party in each state draw maps that protect its own seats. This bill would instead require states with more than one representative to use a five-member redistricting commission. Districts would have to be compact and contiguous, follow local government boundaries where possible, and could not be drawn to favor a political party or to weaken any racial, ethnic, or economic group. Any voter could challenge a plan in federal court.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in states where legislators draw districts to protect incumbents and the majority party. Districts would have to be geographically coherent, follow community lines where possible, and could not be drawn to favor a party, which would make elections more about voters and less about how the map was drawn.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each state with more than one representative to establish a redistricting commission to draw its congressional districts, replacing the current system in which the state legislature draws them [S3].

Sets district standards: districts must be contiguous and compact, must follow local political subdivision boundaries where possible, and may not be drawn to minimize the voting strength of any racial, ethnic, or economic group or to favor any political party [S3].
Gives any eligible voter in a state the right to sue in federal court to enforce these rules, with a three-judge court required to decide the case within 60 days [S3].
Requires commissions to hold public hearings before preparing a plan, and requires the plan to be published in the Federal Register before taking effect [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and the majority parties in state legislatures, who would lose the power to draw their own district lines and with it a major tool for protecting friendly seats. Taxpayers would fund federal grants to the states and the Federal Election Commission to administer the process.

drawbacks.text: The commissions are not independent of politics: legislative leaders appoint four of the five members, and those four choose the chairman, so the same party officials who draw maps today would choose who draws them under the bill [S3].
An unelected commission would take over a core legislative duty currently performed by elected state representatives, removing direct accountability to voters over how districts are drawn [S3].

The ban on drawing districts to avoid minimizing the voting strength of racial, ethnic, or economic groups could collide with districting done to comply with the Voting Rights Act, though the bill lets courts invalidate plans that violate other federal law [S3].
The plan runs through the Federal Election Commission, a campaign-finance agency with no redistricting expertise, which would publish the plans and distribute federal funds to the states [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that legislators should not draw the districts they run in — addresses a real structural conflict of interest, and the enforceable district standards would give voters a tool they lack today. But the design is weak: the commission members are chosen by the very legislative leaders who benefit from gerrymandering, so the reform depends on those leaders picking impartial commissioners. The court-enforcement mechanism is the bill's strongest feature.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee never took the bill up after referring it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Sensenbrenner introduced the bill on April 5, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Judiciary [S1].
Five House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The action history shows only two entries — introduction and referral to Judiciary — with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the state legislators who keep the power to draw congressional district lines. Nothing changed: the existing system, in which the majority party in each state legislature draws its own congressional maps, remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent legislators who keep map-drawing power

for.name: F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Jack Brooks (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters — the sponsor and five cosponsors — were Republicans, with no Democratic cosponsors, and the Democratic-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators
industries.note: Legislators currently draw the congressional districts they and their colleagues run in, and the majority party can use that power to protect its seats. The bill would strip that power and give voters a court remedy against maps drawn to favor a party.

Leadership would lose direct control of map-drawing but would appoint four of the five commission members and choose among themselves who names the chairman, so the bill leaves party leaders substantial influence over the maps.
